slides.1.title: 🎓 Exam Instructions
slides.1.points.0: This exam covers all Level 1 content across 5 modules

slides.2.question: Which of Australia's six states is the most important wine-producing state by volume?
slides.2.explanation: South Australia (SA) produces approximately 50% of all Australian wine. It is home to iconic regions including Barossa Valley, Clare Valley, McLaren Vale and Coonawarra.
slides.3.question: What does GI stand for in Australian wine law?
slides.3.explanation: GI stands for Geographical Indication — Australia's equivalent of an appellation system. It guarantees that a minimum percentage (85%) of the grapes come from the named region.
slides.4.question: Barossa Valley has some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines. What is the main reason phylloxera never reached Barossa?
slides.4.options.0: The soil is too sandy for the louse to survive
slides.4.options.1: A geographical barrier (the Murray River) prevented spread
slides.4.options.2: Strict quarantine measures have always prevented phylloxera from entering South Australia
slides.4.explanation: Strict quarantine controls have kept phylloxera out of South Australia. As a result, Barossa vines can remain on their own roots indefinitely — some are now over 170 years old. This is the foundation of Barossa's old-vine legend.
slides.5.question: Clare Valley Riesling is known for its signature flavour profile. Which best describes a young Clare Valley Riesling?
slides.5.options.1: Squeezed lime juice, slate mineral, razor-sharp acidity
slides.5.explanation: Clare Valley Riesling is Australia's most distinctive Riesling style — intensely citrusy (squeezed lime, lime zest) with a characteristic slate/mineral backbone and extreme natural acidity. This acidity allows it to age for 15–20+ years, developing petrol and toast complexity.
slides.6.question: Hunter Valley Sémillon is harvested at 10–11% potential alcohol. What is the main reason for this early picking?
slides.6.options.1: To preserve extreme natural acidity, allowing the wine to age magnificently in bottle for 15–20 years
slides.6.options.2: Because the grapes stop ripening at this point
slides.6.options.3: To comply with Hunter Valley regulations
slides.6.explanation: Early harvesting preserves Hunter Sémillon's extreme natural acidity. This high acid content acts as a natural preservative, allowing the wine to develop honey, toast and beeswax complexity in bottle over 15–20 years — all without any oak contact.
slides.7.question: Margaret River is often called 'the Bordeaux of Australia'. Which statement best explains this nickname?
slides.7.options.0: It produces the same wine styles as Bordeaux using the same varieties and a similar maritime-influenced climate
slides.7.options.1: A French company owns all the wineries
slides.7.options.2: It exports more wine to France than any other region
slides.7.options.3: The local currency is the euro
slides.7.explanation: Margaret River shares several characteristics with Bordeaux: a gravelly loam soil structure, a maritime-influenced climate (warm dry summers, cool winters), and the same core varieties (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sémillon). The region produces world-class Cabernet-based reds and the famous SBS (Sauvignon Blanc-Sémillon) blend.
slides.8.question: What is the 'terra rossa' soil of Coonawarra, and why is it important for Cabernet Sauvignon?
slides.8.options.0: A deep, moisture-retaining clay that helps vines stay hydrated
slides.8.options.1: Red iron-rich topsoil over free-draining limestone that stresses vines, concentrating flavours and giving Cabernet a distinctive mint and blackcurrant character
slides.8.options.2: A sandy soil imported from Italy
slides.8.options.3: A volcanic soil found throughout South Australia
slides.8.explanation: Terra rossa is iron-oxidised red topsoil sitting over free-draining limestone. The combination forces vine roots deep into the limestone for moisture and minerals while surface drainage prevents waterlogging. The resulting Cabernet Sauvignon is structured, with distinctive mint/eucalyptus and blackcurrant flavours — unique to Coonawarra's narrow terra rossa strip.
slides.9.question: Rutherglen Muscat has four quality tiers. Which is the most concentrated and oldest?
slides.9.explanation: Rutherglen Muscat's four tiers (Rutherglen → Classic → Grand → Rare) represent increasing age and concentration. 'Rare' contains the oldest barrel stocks — sometimes 25+ years old — producing extraordinary complexity of coffee, dark caramel, Christmas pudding and rancio nuttiness.
slides.10.question: Tasmania is considered the future of premium Australian wine. What is the primary reason for this?
slides.10.options.0: It has the cheapest land in Australia
slides.10.options.1: Its cool maritime climate (the coolest in Australia) is perfect for high-acid sparkling wine base and elegant Pinot Noir, and becomes more valuable as the mainland warms due to climate change
slides.10.options.2: It produces the most wine by volume
slides.10.options.3: It has the most established wine history
slides.10.explanation: Tasmania's proximity to Antarctica and exposure to Southern Ocean air currents make it Australia's coolest wine region by far. This cool climate preserves natural acidity — essential for world-class sparkling wine and elegant Pinot Noir. As mainland Australia warms, Tasmania's cool-climate advantage becomes increasingly strategic.
